SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                Suffix: PUC
PUC Docket No. 59475



             Before the
   State Office of Administrative
              Hearings


  JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY
   COMPANY LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES
  CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF
 CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY
     EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION 765-KV
    TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET,
    CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS, LLANO, MASON,
    MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA,
SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN, AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES




                          SOAH ORDER NO. 13
      DENYING MOTIONS FOR ROUTE ADEQUACY HEARING AND
               CANCELING ROUTE ADEQUACY HEARING


      Brady M. Johnson, Dub Z. Johnson, and Jeri Johnson Willoughby (the
Johnson Intervenors); the Burnet County Commissioners Court; Save the Lampasas
(an aligned group of intervenors); and 4K Land and Cattle Company filed timely
requests for a route adequacy hearing. The requests are supported by:
 Suzanne C. James and Bruce L. James, and Reata River Ranch, LP; Deborah Nobles,
Gerald C. Nobles, Jr., and the L Bar Family Ranch, LP; and G-9 and G-13
Landowners. Oncor Electric Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services
Corporation (collectively, Applicants) filed a timely response to the motions. For the
reasons discussed below, the requests for route adequacy hearing are DENIED and
the route adequacy hearing scheduled for May 18, 2026, is CANCELED.


I.    BACKGROUND AND LEGAL AUTHORITY

      On March 26, 2026, Applicants filed an application (Application) with the
Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) to amend their certificates of
convenience and necessity (CCN) for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill
Substation 765-kilovolt (kV) transmission line project in Bell, Burnet, Concho,
Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba,
Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson Counties.


      In its Order of Referral and Preliminary Order referring this case to the State
Office of Administrative Hearings, the Commission included the following issue to
be addressed:

      Is the applicant’s joint application to amend its CCNs adequate? Does
      the joint application contain an adequate number of reasonably
      differentiated alternative routes to conduct a proper evaluation? In
      answering this question, consideration must be given to the number of
      proposed transmission facilities that influence the location of the line.
      Consideration may also be given to the facts and circumstances specific
      to the geographic area under consideration and to any analysis and
      reasoned justification presented for a limited number of alternative
      routes. A limited number of alternative routes is not in itself a sufficient
      basis for finding an application inadequate when the facts and
                                             2
                                   SOAH Order No. 13
                     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349, PUC Docket No. 59475
          circumstances or a reasoned justification demonstrates a reasonable
         basis for presenting a limited number of alternatives. If an adequate
         number of routes is not presented in the joint application, the ALJ must
         allow applicants to amend the joint application and to provide proper
         notice to affected landowners; however, if the applicants choose not to
         amend the joint application, then the ALJ may dismiss the case without
         prejudice.


         Applicants bear the burden of proof to establish that the routes presented in
the Application are adequate.1


II.      REQUESTS FOR ROUTE ADEQUACY HEARING

         The Johnson Intervenors’ request for route adequacy hearing challenges “the
adequacy of any proposed route combination that includes or relies upon Link V1, or
any segment that crosses or parallels the San Saba River corridor in proximity to
Intervenors’ property, including Tracts 4605 and 4606.”


         4K Land and Cattle Company states that the Application confines a 214- to
244-mile unprecedented 765-kV project to a narrow study area which spans only
about 35 miles north-to-south and funnels alternatives into a few convergent
corridors, fails to consult Texas Parks and Wildlife Department resources,
disregards recognized EPRI-GTC industry framework, fails to use available public
data, departs from established analytical process for siting decisions of this
magnitude, and relies on aerial reconnaissance as the principal analytical method.



1 Application of Wood County Electric Cooperative, Inc. for a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for a Proposed

Transmission Line in Wood County, Texas, Docket No. 32070, Order on Appeal of Order No. 8 at 6 (Oct. 31, 2006).
                                                         3
                                           SOAH Order No. 13
                             SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349, PUC Docket No. 59475
 The Centerline Gravity Index (CGI)2 in this case is 3.37%, compared to 5.02% for the
Dinosaur-Longshore proceeding with the same applicants. 4K Land and Cattle
Company identifies the northern periphery of the study area as a ripe but
unexamined alternative corridor. Only one “northern corridor” characterized by
Link U6 was included.3 The Application did not investigate any route further north
(for example, angling from Big Hill Substation up into Coleman, Brown, or Mills
County before heading east toward Bell County). According to 4K Land and Cattle
Company, without a northern or otherwise significantly different corridor, the
Commission cannot be assured the selected route is truly the best one.


         The Burnet County Commissioners Court argues that the Applicants failed to
identify and evaluate a reasonable range of geographically diverse alternative because
all routes cross some part of Burnet County. It posits that the exclusion of routing
alternatives to the north shows the Applicants’ routing options lack diversity. The
Burnet County Commissioners Court proposes two additional routes which utilize
existing highway corridors and rights of way.


         Save the Lampasas contends that the routing options in eastern Burnet
County are limited to three link corridors, creating a bottleneck, and do not follow
any compatible infrastructure, including rights-of-way, transportation corridors, or
property lines. Save the Lampasas urges that an alternative segment in the southern
portion of the study area that parallels an existing transmission line in the area would


2 CGI is a length-weighted measure of how far the segments of an alternatives universe sit, on average, from the

straight-line endpoint connection.
3 Application at Attachment 11 (Routing Memo).

                                                       4
                                           SOAH Order No. 13
                             SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349, PUC Docket No. 59475
 parallel existing infrastructure. Save the Lampasas posits that routing options north
of Fort Hood should have been included and that Highways 183 and 281 could be
routing corridors available for consideration.


III.   APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE

       In response, Applicants begin by noting that the Application includes
122 geographically diverse routes, comprised of 171 alternative route links. These
routes offer thousands of potential pathways to connect the Project’s endpoints,
covering a geographic area that spans approximately 200 miles east-to-west and
35 miles north-to-south. In Applicants’ view, the extent of the options provided
creates a prima facie showing that the Application provides an adequate number of
reasonably differentiated alternative routes to conduct a proper evaluation.


       While the specifics of the route adequacy challenges vary, Applicants maintain
that they should be denied because they do not actually call into question whether
Applicants proposed an adequate number of routes. As an initial matter, Applicants
note that criticisms of individual routes or links contained in the Application—as
made by the Johnson Intervenors—are not proper route adequacy challenges. A
route adequacy challenge considers wither the application contains an adequate
number of reasonably differentiated alternative routes to conduct a proper
evaluation, whereas challenges to specific links are an issue to be addressed at the
hearing on the merits.


       Next, Applicants explain that the size of the study area is justified by existing
constraints. The ALJs generally find these arguments persuasive, and they are
                                              5
                                    SOAH Order No. 13
                      SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349, PUC Docket No. 59475
 described in the Analysis section below. Further, despite these constraints,
Applicants challenge the characterization of the proposed routes as having
“chokepoints.” During their route-evaluation process, Applicants grouped routes
into five discernable corridors based on each route’s use of five individual links. With
five separate corridor groups over a 35-mile north-to-south study area, Applicants
argue that no “chokepoints” were created as a result of their route evaluation
process.


IV.      ANALYSIS AND RULING

         The purpose of a preliminary route-adequacy hearing is to perform a more
cursory review of the application to determine whether it contains an adequate
justification for the routes selected and whether additional routes should be added at
an early stage in the contested case process.4 A route adequacy challenge focused on
specific proposed routes that would impact the intervenor’s property but that does
not contend the proposed routes lack differentiation or geographic diversity does not
properly assert a route adequacy challenge.5 Once an applicant makes a prima facie
showing that its application is adequate, the parties challenging route adequacy
“must present evidence showing the inadequacy of an application or routes and




4 Application of Brazos Electric Power Cooperative, Inc., to Amend its Certificate of Convenience and Necessity (CCN) for a

Proposed 138-kV Double Circuit Transmission Line and Substation in Collin County, Texas, Docket No. 34276, SOAH
Order No. 22 at 9 (Feb. 19, 2008).
5 Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation to Amend their

Certificates of Convenience and Necessity for the Big Hill Substation to Sand Lake Switch 765-kV Transmission Line Project
in Crane, Crockett, Irion, Pecos, Reagan, Reeves, Schleicher, Tom Green, Upton, and Ward Counties, Docket No. 59182,
SOAH Order No. 8 (Mar. 2, 2026).
                                                            6
                                             SOAH Order No. 13
                               SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349, PUC Docket No. 59475
 presenting other superior routes.”6 The applicants can then rebut this evidence by
offering a reasoned justification as to why any proposed alternative routes should not
be included.7 An applicant is not required to disprove the viability of every
conceivable routing permutation developed by other parties.8


         4K Land and Cattle Company, Burnet County Commissioners Court, and
Save the Lampasas argued that additional routes to the north should be added.
However, Applicants persuasively explained how geographic and regulatory
constraints limit that as a feasible or cost-effective option. The Bell County East
Switch and Big Hill Substation sit at approximately the same latitude, so routes that
swing far north (around Fort Hood) or south (around Lake Buchanon) would
necessarily double-back, increasing mileage and costs, and running contrary to the
requirement that routing alternatives be reasonably forward progressing.


         To the north, the Project cannot cross Fort Hood without obtaining prior
federal government approval, which Applicants cannot obtain.9 Any routes pushed
further north are likely to introduce military aviation conflicts, such as impacts to
airspace, aviation training, or operations of Fort Hood.10 Surrounding Fort Hood is



6 Application of Southwestern Public Service Company to Amend a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for a Proposed

230-kV Transmission Line within Lubbock County (Wolfforth to Carlisle), Docket No. 42729, SOAH Order No. 6 at 4
(Dec. 22, 2014).
7 Application of LCRA Transmission Service Corporation to Amend its Certificate of Convenience and Necessity (CCN) for a

138 kV Transmission Line in Kerr County, Docket No. 33844, SOAH Order No. 10 at 3 (Jul. 30, 2007).
8 Docket No. 33844, SOAH Order No. 10 at 3-4.

9 See Application, Attachment 1 – Appendix A at A-1022 through A-1029 (Item No. 65).

10 See Application, Attachment 1 – Appendix A at 1022, 1027, 1028 (Item No. 65).

                                                           7
                                            SOAH Order No. 13
                              SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349, PUC Docket No. 59475
 dense commercial and residential areas, including Temple, Belton, Killeen, Harker
Heights, and Copperas Cove, which could not be realistically crossed by a 200-foot
right-of-way for a 765-kV transmission line without the removal of likely hundreds
or thousands of homes and other structures.11 Additionally, Applicants evaluated the
corridors at Lake Belton and Stillhouse Hollow Lake at the northeast corner of the
study area, but none had adequate space for the proposed transmission line right-of-
way.12


         To the south, Lake Buchanan, one of the largest lakes in Texas, is five miles
wide at points. Due to the lake’s size, the proposed project cannot cross Lake
Buchanan. Immediately to the south of Lake Buchanan is Inks Lake and Lake LBJ
and extensive commercial and residential development associated with these three
lakes. Farther southeast of Lake Buchanan is the Balcones Canyonlands National
Wildlife Refuge. As such, any alterative routes south of Lake Buchanan would not be
superior to the routes presented in the Application.


         The fact that all routes use a limited number of corridors does not necessarily
demonstrate an inadequate number of routes in the Application. In Docket
No. 41606, all routes were routed through one of two links: 137b or 84b. The ALJ
found that the applicants in that case “presented sufficient evidence that the small
chokepoints are driven by area constraints, and thus, are reasonable given the overall




11 See Applicants Response, Exhibit 1.

12 See Applicants Response, Exhibit 1.

                                                     8
                                           SOAH Order No. 13
                             SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349, PUC Docket No. 59475
 length of the proposed transmission line.”13 Here, the routes are grouped into five
corridors rather than only two, and Applicants have established the specific
geographic and regulatory constraints that shaped such corridors.


         4K Land and Cattle Company's concerns about the use of Texas Parks and
Wildlife Department resources and recognized EPRI-GTC industry framework do
not pertain to the adequacy of alternative routes in the Application. Therefore, they
are not further addressed in this Order.


         The Johnson Intervenors’ concerns relate to routes that would affect their
properties and are more appropriately addressed at the hearing on the merits rather
than a route adequacy hearing.


         The ALJs find that the Application provides an adequate number of
reasonably differentiated alternative routes to conduct a proper evaluation.
Applicant has established facts and circumstances specific to the study area and
provided a reasoned justification for the alternative routes presented. The requests
for route adequacy hearing are DENIED, and the route adequacy hearing scheduled
for May 18, 2026, is CANCELED.




13 Joint Application of Electric Transmission Texas, LLC and Sharyland Utilities, L.P. to Amend their Certificates of

Convenience and Necessity for the North Edinburg to Loma Alta Double-Circuit 345-kV Transmission Line in Hidalgo and
Cameron Counties, Docket No. 41606, SOAH Order No. 6 at 24 (Oct. 21, 2013).

 Signed May 15, 2026
